Annelida. A phylum of invertebrate segmented worms including earthworms, leeches, and marine bristle worms. They're characterized by metamerism—their bodies are divided into repeated segments, each containing identical organs and separated internally by membranous walls called septa. They possess a closed circulatory system and are found in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial habitats everywhere.

The defining feature is their segmentation. Those chitinous bristles called setae project from their skin, and the worms use them to anchor themselves and move through soil and water. Another distinctive structure is the clitellum, that prominent glandular ring you see near the head of earthworms and leeches. It secretes a sticky cocoon that protects fertilized eggs. Then there are leeches themselves, which are blood-feeding ectoparasites that secrete an incredibly powerful anticoagulant called hirudin to keep their host's blood flowing while they feed.

The closed circulatory system is the height of sophistication for a worm. They use a network of blood vessels and five pairs of muscular loop vessels that act as hearts, pumping blood through the entire organism. This distinguishes them from their relatives in other phyla. Mollusks, while they share a similar ciliated marine larval stage called a trochophore, lack the segmented bodies that define annelids. Roundworms, or nematodes, are unsegmented pseudocoelomates entirely different in body plan. And flatworms are unsegmented acoelomates without even the basic divisions that annelids possess.
